items.stem: Evaluate Maslow’s hierarchy of needs as an explanation of motivation at work, including a discussion of cultural bias.
items.answer: Strength (usefulness): It reminds managers that pay and security must be provided before esteem and growth rewards will motivate. Strength (face validity): The idea that basic needs come first matches everyday experience and is easy to understand. Weakness (empirical support): Research has found little evidence for five distinct levels or a strict order of satisfaction. Weakness (cultural bias): It reflects individualist Western values; in collectivist cultures belonging may be more important than self-actualisation. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement about the overall value of the study.

items.stem: Discuss the extent to which money is the most important motivator at work. In your answer, you may refer to intrinsic versus extrinsic motivation and individual differences.
items.answer: Arguments for: Pay meets physiological and security needs and can be linked to performance through bonuses and performance-related pay. In VIE theory, pay often has high valence for employees. Arguments against: Herzberg classed pay as a hygiene factor that prevents dissatisfaction but does not motivate. Deci (1971) found that paying people for an interesting task reduced their intrinsic motivation. Recognition, responsibility and interesting work also motivate. Conclusion: a supported judgement weighing the evidence on both sides.

items.stem: Discuss the strengths and weaknesses of Vroom’s expectancy (VIE) theory. Include at least one point about usefulness.
items.answer: Strength (usefulness): Managers can identify which component is low (for example unclear link between performance and reward) and fix it. Strength (individual differences): It recognises that different employees value different rewards. Weakness (measurement): Expectancy, instrumentality and valence are subjective and hard to measure accurately. Weakness (rationality): It assumes people calculate probabilities and values rationally, but many decisions are emotional or habitual. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement about the overall value of the study.

items.stem: Assess the view that need theories provide the best explanation of motivation at work. In your answer, you may refer to individual differences and usefulness.
items.answer: Arguments for: Maslow, Alderfer and McClelland explain why people want different things from work (security, relationships, growth, achievement). They are easy for managers to apply, for example by offering security before esteem rewards. Arguments against: There is little evidence for a fixed hierarchy of needs; people pursue several needs at once (Alderfer’s ERG theory). Cognitive theories (goal-setting, VIE) explain how people choose how much effort to put in, which need theories ignore. Needs are hard to measure objectively and vary between cultures. Conclusion: a supported judgement weighing the evidence on both sides.

items.stem: Discuss the strengths and weaknesses of Deci’s (1971) laboratory study of rewards and intrinsic motivation. Include at least one point about objective measure.
items.answer: Strength (controls): A control group was never paid, so the change in free-choice time can be attributed to payment. Strength (objective measure): Time spent on puzzles in the free-choice period was measured covertly, reducing demand characteristics. Weakness (ecological validity): Solving puzzles for $1 in a laboratory is very different from long-term pay at work. Weakness (generalisability): Participants were university students, so the findings may not apply to employees who need their wage. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement about the overall value of the study.

items.answer: (a) Specific goal: 5; do-your-best: 11. (b) The specific goal condition had a higher mean (50.6) than the do-your-best condition (45.0), suggesting that setting specific, difficult goals increases performance.

items.stem: Evaluate Deci’s (1971) laboratory study of rewards and intrinsic motivation, including a discussion of generalisability.
items.answer: Strength (objective measure): Time spent on puzzles in the free-choice period was measured covertly, reducing demand characteristics. Strength (controls): A control group was never paid, so the change in free-choice time can be attributed to payment. Weakness (generalisability): Participants were university students, so the findings may not apply to employees who need their wage. Weakness (ecological validity): Solving puzzles for $1 in a laboratory is very different from long-term pay at work. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement about the overall value of the study.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. Top band: strengths and weaknesses are accurate, well explained and clearly linked to the study, the named issue is discussed, the answer is well organised and reaches a conclusion. Middle band: points are mostly accurate but one side is less developed or links to the study are general. Lower band: points are identified but brief, generic or one-sided. Description of the procedure without evaluation receives little credit.

items.stem: Which term is defined as the following: “Alderfer’s theory that people have existence, relatedness and growth needs, which can operate at the same time”?
items.answer: ERG theory

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) In a revision session, a student says: “McClelland suggested that people with high need for achievement prefer extremely difficult tasks.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) Explain two differences between Maslow’s hierarchy of needs and Alderfer’s ERG theory.
items.answer: (a) Not correct. They prefer moderately difficult tasks with a realistic chance of success and clear feedback. (b) Maslow has five levels, ERG has three (existence, relatedness, growth); Maslow says lower needs must be satisfied before higher ones, while ERG allows several needs at once and includes frustration–regression.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: correct judgement; 1 mark: accurate explanation [2] (b) 1 mark each difference, 2 marks maximum each [4]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Describe McClelland’s theory of needs. (b) A student writes: “Maslow’s theory states that a person cannot be motivated by esteem until safety needs are reasonably satisfied.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) People have three learned needs – achievement, affiliation and power – in different strengths. The dominant need shapes behaviour at work: high nAch people like moderately difficult tasks with feedback; high nPow people seek influence; high nAff people seek good relationships. (b) Correct. Lower needs must be largely met first.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark three needs; 1 mark acquired; 1 mark effect on work [3] (b) 1 mark: correct judgement; 1 mark: accurate explanation [2]

items.stem: Omar works in a factory in Riyadh. The pay is fair and the job is secure, but Omar says: “I never learn anything new, and nobody ever notices when I do a good job.” Using ERG theory, explain what might happen if Omar’s growth needs remain blocked.
items.answer: Frustration–regression: Omar may focus more on relatedness or existence needs, for example socialising or asking for more pay.

items.stem: Tomás wants to find out whether being paid for an interesting task reduces intrinsic motivation. Design a laboratory experiment to investigate this. Your plan must include: the type of data collected, ethical issues and how the dependent variable will be measured.
items.answer: Method: a laboratory experiment. Manipulate the IV in a controlled room; standardised procedure and instructions; measure the DV objectively. Variables: IV: paid or not paid; DV: time spent on the task in a free-choice period. Sample: for example an opportunity or volunteer sample of about 30 people from the target population in Santiago, with reasons. Design/procedure: clear, replicable steps, with standardised instructions and random allocation or counterbalancing where relevant. Ethics: informed consent, right to withdraw, protection from harm, confidentiality and a full debrief. Data: quantitative scores summarised with means and a suitable graph; qualitative answers analysed into themes where collected.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. Top band: a detailed, accurate and replicable plan using the stated method; all required features are included and are appropriate to the aim; variables are operationalised; ethics are addressed. Middle band: a workable plan with most required features but some lack detail or are not justified. Lower band: a basic plan with few features or with errors in method.

items.stem: Evaluate Maslow’s hierarchy of needs as an explanation of motivation at work, including a discussion of empirical support.
items.answer: Strength (face validity): The idea that basic needs come first matches everyday experience and is easy to understand. Strength (usefulness): It reminds managers that pay and security must be provided before esteem and growth rewards will motivate. Weakness (empirical support): Research has found little evidence for five distinct levels or a strict order of satisfaction. Weakness (cultural bias): It reflects individualist Western values; in collectivist cultures belonging may be more important than self-actualisation. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement about the overall value of the study.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. Description of the procedure without evaluation receives little credit.

items.stem: Which term is defined as the following: “In VIE theory, the belief that successful performance will lead to a particular outcome or reward”?
items.answer: Instrumentality

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain how goal-setting theory could be used to improve the performance of sales staff. (b) Explain why VIE theory is described as a cognitive theory.
items.answer: (a) Set specific, difficult but achievable sales targets, involve staff in setting them to increase commitment, and give regular feedback on progress. (b) It assumes employees think rationally about the likely results of their effort, estimating probabilities (expectancy, instrumentality) and the value of outcomes (valence) before deciding how hard to work.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark specific/difficult; 1 mark commitment; 1 mark feedback [3] (b) 1 mark rational thinking; 1 mark reference to components [2]

items.stem: A supermarket in Cape Town sets checkout staff the goal of “being friendly to customers”. Performance has not improved. items.answer: (a) It is vague and not measurable, so staff do not know what to aim for or how they are doing. (b) For example: greet every customer and achieve an average customer-feedback score of at least 4.5 out of 5 this month. (c) Feedback lets staff see progress and adjust effort, and maintains commitment.

items.stem: What is meant by ‘extrinsic motivation’?
items.answer: Motivation that comes from external rewards such as pay or praise, or from avoiding punishment.

items.stem: Discuss the extent to which money is the most important motivator at work. In your answer, you may refer to intrinsic versus extrinsic motivation, individual differences and validity of evidence.
items.answer: Arguments for: Pay meets physiological and security needs and can be linked to performance through bonuses and performance-related pay. In VIE theory, pay often has high valence for employees. Arguments against: Herzberg classed pay as a hygiene factor that prevents dissatisfaction but does not motivate. Deci (1971) found that paying people for an interesting task reduced their intrinsic motivation. Recognition, responsibility and interesting work also motivate. Conclusion: a supported judgement weighing the evidence on both sides.
